title: Shantideva's dedication, again
hookLine: reread the last chapter of Shantideva's guide
tomorrow: a nun's whole poem: a mortar, a pestle, and freedom. how?

cards: Open the liner notes of an album, or the first page of a novel, and there's a line before the work begins: for my mother. For the friends who stayed. Sometimes just: for you.
One person, or everyone? Shantideva had to answer that too. He was an Indian monk who wrote a guide to the bodhisattva's way of life, and when the guide is finished, he doesn't sign off.
He gives the whole thing away.

teach.b: The last chapter is the dedication, and it's long. In plain paraphrase: by whatever good came from writing this, may the sick be healed. May the frightened stop being afraid.
May travelers find their way, and the lonely find company.

teach.h: NAMED ONE BY ONE, THEN WIDER.
teach.b: It names people one by one, then it keeps widening, until it reaches a line the tradition holds close: as long as space remains, as long as beings remain, may I remain too, to ease the world's suffering.
So what does a dedication actually do? Here the tradition holds two real views.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: THE GOOD IS TRULY SHARED.
teach.b: One says the good is truly shared. That view stands behind dedicating merit to parents, to the dead, to every being: the good of an act can be given, like a lamp lighting other lamps.
The other says each person's actions are their own, as the Dhammapada puts it, no one purifies another. On this view the dedication works on the one who makes it.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: IT TURNS THE GIVER OUTWARD.
teach.b: It turns the heart outward, so even your best work isn't hoarded.
Hear both out. The first trusts that goodness can travel. The second trusts that it changes you first.

how: A sitting, a chant or a day's study is commonly closed by dedicating its merit to all beings, and in some Tibetan and other Mahayana communities verses from Shantideva's last chapter are recited for it.

o: a closing chapter that gives the book's good away to all
a page thanking the teachers who taught the author
a vow to stay a monk until the end of his life

games.q: inside the dedication — tap the pairs.
p: the monk who wrote the guide
gives the good of the work away

s: Shantideva's dedication names only one person
it names the sick, the frightened, travelers and more, then widens to all beings.
Buddhists agree on exactly how dedicating merit works
some hold the good is truly shared; others hold it works first on the one who dedicates.
the chapter ends with a wish to remain as long as space remains
as long as beings remain, to ease the world's suffering.

games.q: your friend says dedicating your run 'to everyone with cancer' is just words. give the best case for each view.
o: one: the good can travel to them. two: it keeps you running outward, not for yourself.
it's just words, so drop the dedication and only run for your own time
it only counts if you raise money; dedications on their own do nothing
games.why: both views live inside the tradition. one trusts that goodness can be shared; the other that dedicating changes the giver first. neither calls it empty.

practice: Sit with whatever good this reading did, however small. Near the end, turn it outward the way the chapter does: first toward one person you have in mind, then wider, to people you'll never meet.

wordCard.voice: Shantideva's dedication: the last chapter of his guide, giving away the good of the whole work, to named beings and then to all.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dedication, the title of the last chapter of Shantideva's guide, turning the good of an act toward others.

carryVoice: As long as space remains: he finished the book by handing it to everyone. The Mahayana block, done.
